title: Bidirectional BFS in London: Meet in the Middle ⚡
description: See how Bidirectional BFS runs two BFS searches—one from the start and one from the goal—until they meet, dramatically reducing explored nodes. Perfect for graph optimization and coding interview prep.
ig_caption:
Bidirectional BFS: Why Meeting in the Middle Cuts Search Space in Half ⚡ Two simultaneous BFS frontiers launch from start and goal, and the moment they meet, you’ve found the shortest path—without scanning the whole graph. 

How it works (real map intuition):
- Forward BFS expands outward from the start
- Backward BFS expands outward from the goal
- Each step grows a smaller frontier; the explored set shrinks because you’re solving two smaller “half-distance” problems
- When a node appears in both visited sets, reconstruct the path by stitching parents from both sides

Technical nugget (why it’s faster): If the shortest path length is d and the branching factor is b, standard BFS explores ~b^d nodes, while Bidirectional BFS explores ~2·b^(d/2) (meet in the middle), cutting the search space dramatically.

Takeaway: For unweighted graphs/mazes, Bidirectional BFS is a classic graph optimization that can turn a “slow scan” into a targeted convergence.

Debate question: Would you ever use Bidirectional BFS on a weighted graph—or is it strictly an unweighted win? 👀
